column4: One ayah joins the section's two central charges: protect the orphan's property until maturity and give full measure and weight; the guarded child and the honestly filled vessel belong to one justice.
It forbids approaching the orphan's property except beneficially until maturity; 17:35 then moves directly to the full measure, reproducing the section's meeting of orphan-care and a filled measure.
The command to give full measure and weigh justly completes 17:34's rule for orphan property, setting honest filling beside care for the fatherless exactly as the section does.
وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ names the act the house in the section withholds and places the needy and orphan together as its recipients.
موسى and his companion ask a town's people for food, but the people refuse hospitality; this stages the petitioner, stocked household, and withholding hand at an actual door.
The repaired wall belongs to two orphan boys and hides their treasure until they mature; divine guardianship preserves a fatherless household's provision in the town that denied food.
مُنِعَ مِنَّا ٱلْكَيْلُ puts the section's withholding root directly upon a grain measure, fusing its withheld utensil and shaken-full measure in one clause.
The warning to those who defraud in measure judges the same vessel the section imagines being filled; 83:2-3 specify the selfish asymmetry.
They demand a full measure when receiving from people, the acquisitive half of the household selfishness that keeps useful goods and food for itself.
They cause loss when measuring or weighing for others, the exact contrary of shaking a measure until the recipient's vessel is full.
At inheritance division, relatives, orphans, and the needy who are present must receive provision and a kind word; the household door remains open when goods are apportioned.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ repeats the section's failure to urge food for the needy and makes it part of the condemned person's own record.
كَلَّا بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ directly condemns failure to honor the orphan; 89:18 adds the matching refusal to urge feeding.
وَلَا تَحَٰٓضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ closely repeats 107:3 and follows failure toward the orphan, preserving the section's child-and-food sequence.
The people of Saqar confess that they were not among those who prayed; 74:44 immediately pairs that failure with not feeding the needy, matching the surah's prayer-and-pantry test.
وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ is the confessed omission of the act the section's stocked house could perform, paired with neglected prayer in 74:43.
Feeding on a day of severe hunger turns the section's filled dish into help precisely when food is hardest to release; 90:15-16 name its recipients.
The hungry recipient is an orphan of near kin, bringing the fatherless child inside the circle of household relation rather than leaving the child at the door.
The other hungry recipient is a needy person in destitution, completing the same orphan-needy pairing that structures the section.
فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ forbids overpowering the orphan, a direct moral reversal of the hand that forcefully pushes the child away.
وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids rebuffing the person who asks, covering the neighbor who comes for food or a small household implement.
يُدَعُّونَ إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا uses the source section's د ع ع root for forceful shoving; the shover of the orphan is confronted with the same violence as punishment.
مَنُوعًا is the very withholding disposition named by the section's dictionary form; 70:22-25 oppose it with prayer and a recognized share for the deprived.
مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ names the habitual withholder of good, joining the source dictionary's mennāʿ to its explanation of māʿūn as every recognized good.
مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ again makes withholding good a defining charge, not an insignificant choice about a cheap object.
If such people possessed a share of dominion, they would not give others even a naqīr, the speck on a date stone; this is the section's refusal of the tiny, easy thing in Quranic scale.
Even if people owned the treasuries of divine mercy, they would hold back from fear of depletion; it states the false scarcity behind refusing an item that returns and scarcely diminishes the house.
أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ describes one who gives a little and then stops, making the boundary of a tiny kindness itself morally revealing.
When told to spend from God's provision, the unbelievers answer, أَنُطْعِمُ مَن لَّوْ يَشَآءُ ٱللَّهُ أَطْعَمَهُ; the stocked household turns divine provision into its excuse for not feeding.
A family struck by hardship arrives with scant merchandise and asks Joseph to give full measure and be charitable, putting need, request, giver, and brimming measure into one scene.
The command to do good names orphans, the needy, the near neighbor, the distant neighbor, and the traveler; it supplies the full social map of the person arriving at a household door.
This ayah permits eating from one's own and relatives' houses, houses whose keys one holds, and friends' houses; it presents household stores as a shared network of access and trust.
House divorced women where you dwell according to your means, do not constrain them, and support pregnancy; shelter and provision are duties of the household holder.
Each person must spend according to what God has given, and ease follows hardship; measured means define responsible provision without making scarcity an excuse to give nothing.
Command your household to pray and persist, while God says He asks no provision and provides for them; family prayer and household sustenance are held together rather than split apart.
Ishmael commands his household to prayer and almsgiving, the positive household counterpart to prayer that leaves food and useful goods withheld.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and askers alongside prayer; belief is tested through the same household-facing recipients.
Improving the affairs of orphans is best, and mixing life with them makes them brothers; this replaces the expelled child with an orphan incorporated into the household.
Give orphans their property and do not consume it into your own; the guardian's stocked house must release what belongs to the child.
Guardians must provide food and clothing from the property they manage and speak kindly, joining sustaining goods with the respectful welcome also required in 4:8.
Test orphans until marriageable age and then deliver their property without wasteful or hasty consumption; it supplies the maturity boundary in the section's definition of yatīm.
Those who fear leaving vulnerable young children behind must fear God and speak rightly, asking the householder to see an orphan through the vulnerability of his own small dependents.
Consuming orphan property is described as swallowing fire, exposing the violence hidden when a guardian fills his own vessels from a fatherless child's goods.
The ruling demands justice for orphan women denied what is assigned to them and for vulnerable children, extending the section's small fatherless child to household guardianship and property.
The reminder that God found the addressee an orphan and gave shelter makes a dwelling the answer to lost guardianship, directly completing the section's homeless child image.
The covenant places good treatment of orphans and the needy beside kind speech, prayer, and almsgiving, the same union of worship and household-facing care.
Asked what to spend, the answer directs good wealth to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, locating giving in the household's nearest circles and beyond.
People of means are forbidden to swear off giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; it directly checks a well-supplied hand's decision to withhold.
Their wealth contains a right for the asker and the deprived, so the arrival at the door discloses an existing claim rather than requesting an optional leftover.
Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf to visiting messengers; the home answers arrival with prepared food, the direct opposite of the town that refuses two hungry travelers.
Abraham quietly goes to his household and returns with a fat calf, showing the interior store mobilized for guests rather than kept behind the door.
He places the food before the guests and invites them to eat, completing the movement from household provision to the visitor's reach.
A water drawer lowers his bucket and brings the separated boy Joseph up from the well; the source dictionary's loanable bucket becomes an implement that reaches a vulnerable child.

Each guest is given a knife before the women cut their hands; the dictionary's ordinary lendable knife appears as shared table equipment, while the injury marks a real boundary to the claim that such tools are harmless to pass.

Solomon's workers make basin-like dishes and fixed cauldrons, directly supplying the Quranic counterpart to the section's bowls and pots, here enlarged into signs of abundant provision and grateful use.
Joseph places the drinking cup in his brother's bag; a portable household vessel enters the same grain-measure story that the section connects to withheld measure.
The missing royal cup is paired with a camel-load reward and functions within the provision scene, showing one vessel at the junction of drinking ware and measured grain.
God makes houses a سَكَنًا, using the source section's س ك ن root in its concrete household sense: a dwelling is meant to provide settled shelter.
A father owes nursing mothers food and clothing according to what is fair, and neither parent is to be harmed through the child; household sustenance is measured around a small dependent.
Household dependents and children below puberty must ask permission at three private times, giving a concrete interior scene for the section's small children and household members.
When the children reach puberty they ask permission like adults, supplying the same maturity boundary that ends the section's definition of orphanhood.
The disciples ask whether a table spread can be sent from heaven, turning the request for food and a provisioned table into an explicit address to the giver.
They say they wish to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured, naming actual eating rather than possession of unused provision.
Jesus asks for a table from heaven as a recurring feast and calls God the best provider, contrasting divine provision with the human appeal to God as a reason not to feed.
God answers that He will send the table down, completing the request-and-gift movement that the withholding household interrupts.
Whenever Zechariah enters Mary's sanctuary he finds provision with her, and she says it is from God; guardianship, an interior place, and unexpected food meet in one scene.
Public wealth is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so that it does not circulate only among the rich, preventing stocked resources from remaining on one social shelf.
A stated share of spoils belongs to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, making provision for the fatherless and poor a claim on newly acquired goods.
Feeding a needy person is the compensating duty for one unable to fast, so food placed within reach becomes a concrete act of worship.
The expiation feeds ten needy people from the average food one feeds one's own family, explicitly measuring the visitor's dish by the household table.
Feeding sixty needy people is required when the other forms of expiation cannot be performed, again making actual household provision the religious act.
Sacrificial livestock are to be eaten from and used to feed the afflicted poor, turning a household's meat into a shared meal rather than stored abundance.
After mentioning eating, the ayah commands feeding both the contented non-asker and the petitioner, covering those who come to the door and those whose need remains quiet.
Give the relative, the needy, and the traveler their due; the recipient's share is named as a right, not an optional small favor.
Give the relative, the needy, and the traveler their due, a repeated command that directs household means outward to recognizable claimants.
Give full measure and do not be among those who cause loss; it answers the section's shaking-full vessel with an explicit obligation to fill honestly.
Weigh with an even balance, completing the fair-measure scene rather than letting the vessel's appearance conceal a shortfall.
Do not diminish people's things, broadening fair measure from grain to the useful possessions and benefits owed among people.
Shuayb commands full measure and weight and forbids diminishing people's goods, making honest provision part of social repair.
Shuayb forbids deficient measure and weight while acknowledging his people's prosperity, exposing abundance as no excuse for giving others less.
He commands full measure and weight in justice and forbids diminishing people's things, joining the well-filled container to respect for others' goods.
Establish weight justly and do not make the balance deficient; the command gives the filled-vessel image its rule of exactness.
Joseph fully equips his brothers with their provisions before setting the condition about their brother, establishing the granary as a place able to fill a family's containers.
No measure will be given if the brother is not brought, setting the explicit boundary whose later report is مَنَعَ مِنَّا ٱلْكَيْلُ in 12:63.
Joseph has their merchandise returned inside their saddlebags, a material enactment of the section's point that what leaves a generous store may come back.
The brothers discover their goods returned and expect another camel-load, calling it an easy measure; returned goods, added provision, and ease converge on the section's household image.
Constancy in prayer describes those exempted from the withholding impulse of 70:21, contrasting with prayer detached from the pantry's claims.
Their wealth contains a known right, turning what might look like a voluntary small favor into an assigned share.
The known right belongs to the asker and the deprived, naming both the person at the door and the needy person who does not ask.
The immediately preceding surah says God fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them against fear; a community so provisioned is exposed when it will not feed the needy or release a small aid.
The people of the home prefer arriving migrants over themselves despite their own need and are guarded from greed, reversing the stocked house that protects trivial goods from a neighbor.
Who could provide if God withheld His provision? The question reverses 36:47's excuse by making divine supply a reason for humility, not for refusing to feed.
Do not keep the hand chained to the neck or extend it without limit; this gives the image's withholding hand a boundary of responsible household spending.
The servants' spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but balanced, clarifying that opening the household store does not mean destroying its ability to stand.
God is described as feeding while not needing to be fed; this separates the divine provider from the dependent human householder who cites God's will to avoid sharing provision.
Abraham identifies God as the one who feeds and gives drink, locating all filled dishes and cups under received provision rather than private ownership.
God seeks neither provision nor feeding from creatures, marking the limit of the provider analogy: humans feed the needy from what they themselves receive.
No one can withhold mercy God opens or release what He withholds, setting divine control of supply against petty human control of a pot, bucket, or meal.
Solomon is told that God's gift may be bestowed or withheld without account; this exceptional divine authorization marks the opposite boundary from ordinary people's accountable withholding.
Righteousness is not reached until people spend from what they love, reversing the instinct to lend only what is negligible or fill another's dish only after keeping the desired food.
The feeders say they act for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, giving the inner stance opposite to display and possessive calculation over household goods.
Spending and being protected from the soul's greed describe success, naming the inward release required before the hand will take a useful thing down from the shelf.
Those called to spend who are stingy are stingy only against themselves, overturning the householder's belief that withholding preserves his household.
The hypocrites command others not to spend on those with the Messenger so they will disperse; deliberately closing provision becomes a means of driving needy people away.
The hypocrites close their hands, a bodily picture of the same hand that refuses the small object or food despite having it within reach.
Those who are stingy with what God gave them mistake withholding for good, directly challenging the belief that retained stores secure the house.
The condemned are stingy, command others to stinginess, and conceal what God gave them, echoing the person who neither feeds nor urges feeding.
Those who are stingy and command people to stinginess reproduce both failures in the section: the closed hand and the refusal to encourage provision for the needy.
After God grants bounty, they become stingy and turn away, showing how a filled store can harden into the very withholding the gift should have ended.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed; the section's tiny, easy kindness is therefore small in cost but not in moral weight.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, supporting the section's insistence that a trivial household favor remains a real act.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; like 4:8, it keeps material provision and maʿrūf speech under one ethic.
Whatever is spent, God replaces it; this gives theological force to the section's observation that releasing a useful object or provision need not diminish the home.
Spending is likened to a grain producing many ears, transforming the section's individual grains in a filled measure into an image of provision multiplied by release.
When asked what to spend, the answer is the surplus, a precise bridge to lending or giving what the house can release without ceasing to stand.
The one who gives and remains mindful begins the sequence leading toward ease, opposing the hand that withholds the section's easy little thing.
God eases the giver toward ease; the repeated ease makes a moral counterpart to the source dictionary's description of maʿn as a slight, easy thing.
The person who is stingy and imagines himself self-sufficient embodies the house that treats its stored provision as private independence.
The miser is eased toward hardship, reversing his assumption that keeping the easy, little object makes life secure.
Those who mock believers able to give only their effort are condemned, protecting the moral value of a genuinely small contribution from contempt.
The poor restrained in God's cause do not ask importunately and may be mistaken for self-sufficient; the household must notice need beyond the neighbor who knocks.
Give from the good things acquired and do not select defective goods one would accept only reluctantly, applying a quality test to what comes off the household shelf.
One form of hunting expiation is food for needy people, another concrete setting in which edible household value is transferred to the poor.
Obligatory alms are assigned to the poor and needy among named recipients, placing stored wealth under claims outside its owner's household.
The servant explains that he damaged a boat belonging to needy workers to save it from seizure; in the same interpretive sequence as 18:82, a poor household's useful asset is secretly preserved.
The sleepers send one companion with silver to find wholesome food and bring provision back, a compact household-like scene of entrusted money, procurement, and shared food.
Rules for entering the Prophet's houses for a meal protect both hospitality and household privacy, setting a boundary around access to a home's prepared food.
Silver vessels and cups are circulated among the righteous, a concrete positive image of containers moving between hands instead of remaining unused on a shelf.
The vessels are precisely measured, joining the section's container and full-measure images in the continuation of the surah that earlier praised feeding the needy and orphan.
Golden plates and cups are passed around in Paradise; the costly setting magnifies the ordinary social motion the section asks of cheap household ware.
People pass a cup among one another, making shared use of a vessel the scene's central action rather than private retention.
فِى غَمْرَةٍ سَاهُونَ repeats the source section's س ه و wording in its Quranic sense of heedlessness, marking the lexical boundary across which the commentary also hears a porch or rack.
Spouses are created so one may find سَكَن in the other, extending the section's dwelling root from the physical house to the repose that should characterize its relationships.
The spouse is made so the human being may dwell in tranquility with her, another household sense of the section's س ك ن root beyond a building or stored ration.
God apportions the earth's sustenance for those who ask, scaling the section's household provisions up to a measured world intended for claimants.
Do not kill children because of poverty, for God provides for parent and child; fear of an empty pantry cannot erase the dependent child's claim.
Do not kill children for fear of poverty, for God provides for them and their parents; anticipated scarcity is rejected as a reason to close provision against small dependents.
The parable asks the reader to imagine a garden destroyed when its owner has weak young children, making the fragility of dependents and the loss of household sustenance emotionally concrete.
The good loan to God is multiplied on return, a theological analogue to the section's loaned household object that leaves the hand yet is not finally lost.
The promise to multiply a good loan to God reframes release from possession as recoverable gain, challenging anxiety over lending a small useful thing.
Charitable men and women are described as lending God a good loan that is multiplied, joining actual giving to the section's ordinary logic of a borrowed item returned.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, supplying the promised return that the householder fails to trust when guarding trivial goods.
Those who do not give the purifying due are condemned, a broader legal instance of retaining a benefit that is owed beyond oneself.
Cups, pitchers, and a filled drinking vessel are carried in Paradise; the object match with the section's shelf of containers is exact, though this ayah does not itself concern household generosity.
Cups are set ready for use, a plausible visual counterpart to utensils taken down and made available; the surrounding scene is Paradise rather than a neighbor's house.
Night is made سَكَنًا, using the source section's dwelling root for repose rather than a house; it weakly clarifies the rest and stability underlying the household sense.
